5: (1) One who cooks on Shabbos — {or who performed one of the other melachos (Tur)} — intentionally (b'meizid): it is forbidden to him forever, and for others it is permitted immediately after Shabbos. Unintentionally (b'shogeg): it is forbidden that day even for others, and in the evening it is permitted even for him immediately. {And if he told a non-Jew to perform a melacha on Shabbos, see above siman 307 seif 20.}
8: (1) 'Permitted immediately after Shabbos' — for we only require b'chedi she'ya'asu for a melacha performed by a non-Jew on behalf of a Jew, since it is light in his eyes and he may come to do so again. But something a Jew does with his own hands, there is certainly no concern that he will come to cook outright.
11: (1) 'Forbidden to him forever' — it is implied from the Rashba siman 175 that the pot is also forbidden.
13: (3) 'B'shogeg' — one who acted on the instruction of a sage is considered shogeg, and the same applies to one who forgot [so it is in the Radbaz, Beis 26, part 2].
15: (2) 'Permitted immediately after Motzei Shabbos' — specifically when a non-Jew performs the act do we require b'chedi she'ya'asu, since we fear he may tell him to do it again, but a Jew will not listen to him — Tosafos Chullin 15. And if Motzei Shabbos was Yom Tov it is forbidden, for Shabbos does not prepare for Yom Tov [Likkutei Mahariv siman 2]. And if that item became mixed with others, see the Magen Avraham.
17: (3) 'B'shogeg' — if he acted on the instruction of a sage he is considered shogeg, and the same applies to one who forgot — Knesset HaGedolah, Radbaz.
20: (1) Seif 1, 'One who cooks on Shabbos, etc.' — the Shulchan Aruch ruled like R' Yehuda and not R' Meir, because the unattributed ruling in Chullin follows his view. But Tosafos and those who agree with them ruled like R' Meir, and their proof is very clear. And what they wrote — that the unattributed ruling in Chullin follows R' Yehuda — this does not necessarily hold, since the unattributed ruling in chapter 2 of Terumos follows R' Meir, and likewise the sugya at the beginning of chapter 3 of Shabbos. And we rule like R' Yochanan who holds the halacha follows R' Yehuda.
22: (3) 'Immediately' — not like Rashi in Chullin 15a, nor the Baal HaMaor, who explained that b'chedi she'ya'asu is required; Tosafos in the third chapter of Yom Tov disagrees with them and holds that we rule like R' Shimon that muktzeh does not apply, and here there is a distinction between shogeg and meizid.
25: 'One of the other melachos' — the Chayei Adam, klal 9, writes that this applies specifically where an action was performed upon the object itself whereby it was changed from its original state, as in cooking and similar cases. But one who carries from domain to domain — where the object was not changed — if b'shogeg it is permitted even to him even on that same day, and if b'meizid it is forbidden even to others until Motzei Shabbos immediately. Nevertheless one should be stringent in all Torah-level prohibitions as with cooking. And know that according to the Shulchan Aruch who ruled like R' Yehuda that b'shogeg it is permitted to benefit at Motzei Shabbos — this applies to all melachos where the penalty imposed by the Sages not to benefit on that day until Motzei Shabbos is noticeable. But for one who plants on Shabbos, and the same for one who sows, where in any case he cannot benefit immediately — shogeg equals meizid, and in both cases the planting must be uprooted, as stated explicitly in Gittin 54b in the opinion of R' Yehuda.
54: (1) Introduction to the seif — the Torah forbade performing melacha on Shabbos, and one who performed a melacha on Shabbos b'meizid is liable to death and kares, and b'shogeg is liable to a chatas. The Torah's prohibition is upon the person alone, and not upon the item made on Shabbos in a forbidden manner; however the Sages penalized one who performs a melacha on Shabbos and forbade also the item upon which the melacha was performed, so that people should not treat Shabbos prohibitions lightly. The laws of the penalty are explained in this seif.
56: (2) 'Of the other melachos' — meaning: this seif deals with one who performed any of the melachos forbidden by the Torah on Shabbos, and cooking is only an example. This principle is agreed upon also by the Mechaber.
60: (4) 'After Shabbos' — even if the prohibition was done for their sake. For the Sages did not forbid the item forever, but only upon the one who himself desecrated Shabbos. And the vessels in which he cooked on Shabbos in a forbidden manner are not forbidden.
62: (5) 'Immediately' — and there is no need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu, meaning one does not need to wait after Shabbos until the amount of time it would have taken to perform this melacha had they begun it at the conclusion of Shabbos, as the Rama explains further in the seif.
64: (6) 'Immediately' — meaning: b'shogeg the Sages forbade on that Shabbos itself, so that people should not come to treat Shabbos prohibitions lightly; however they did not distinguish between the shogeg himself and others. All this is in a Torah-level melacha. And in a rabbinic melacha: b'meizid it is forbidden like a Torah-level melacha, however if he acted b'shogeg in a rabbinic melacha — it is permitted to benefit from it even on that Shabbos itself.
66: All this applies to a Torah-level melacha. In a rabbinic melacha: b'meizid it is forbidden like a Torah-level melacha, but if he acted b'shogeg in a rabbinic melacha — it is permitted to benefit from it even on that Shabbos itself.
68: (7) 'Siman 307 seif 20' — there it is explained that regarding the prohibition of instructing a non-Jew the Sages were more stringent, and they forbade benefit from Shabbos labor until Motzei Shabbos b'chedi she'ya'asu. And the reason is that the Sages were more stringent regarding the lighter prohibition of instructing a non-Jew, since they were more concerned that people would come to treat it lightly.
